cards.back: To combine or collect into a whole; the total amount. "The aggregate score across all tests determines your final grade." Common collocations: aggregate data, aggregate demand, in aggregate.

Equipment or machinery designed for a particular purpose; a complex system or organization. "The laboratory apparatus was carefully calibrated before the experiment." Common collocations: scientific apparatus, state apparatus, breathing apparatus.
To add something as an attachment or supplement. "Please append your signature to the bottom of the document." Common collocations: append a note, append information, append to a file.

A sphere of activity, debate, or conflict; a central area for sports or performances. "The political arena has become increasingly polarized." Common collocations: public arena, political arena, international arena.

An impressive display or range of things; to arrange in a particular way. "The museum offered an array of artifacts from ancient civilizations." Common collocations: wide array, vast array, array of options.

To state a fact or belief confidently and forcefully. "The researcher asserted that climate change poses immediate threats." Common collocations: assert authority, assert one's rights, assert confidently.

To allocate a task or duty to someone; to designate for a specific purpose. "The teacher assigned homework to be completed by Friday." Common collocations: assign tasks, assign roles, assign responsibility.

A connection or relationship between people or things; to form a close relationship. "The shared experience created a strong bond between the team members." Common collocations: strong bond, emotional bond, bond together.

A system of government or organization with many complicated rules and procedures. "Excessive bureaucracy can slow down decision-making processes." Common collocations: government bureaucracy, reduce bureaucracy, bureaucratic procedures.

A written document that describes rights, principles, or functions of an organization. "The company's charter outlines its core values and mission." Common collocations: charter document, charter member, royal charter.
Persisting for a long time or constantly recurring. "Chronic unemployment remains a serious problem in rural areas." Common collocations: chronic illness, chronic problem, chronic pain.

A closed path through which electricity flows; a regular journey around a particular area. "The electrical circuit was damaged during the storm." Common collocations: electrical circuit, circuit board, complete a circuit.

A particular section of a legal document or contract; a grammatical unit. "The contract includes a clause about confidentiality." Common collocations: contract clause, main clause, subordinate clause.
To force or oblige someone to do something. "The evidence compelled the jury to reach a guilty verdict." Common collocations: compel someone, feel compelled, compel action.
Permission or agreement for something to happen. "Participants must give informed consent before joining the study." Common collocations: give consent, informed consent, mutual consent.

The process of seeking advice or information from experts or stakeholders. "The government held a public consultation on the proposed policy changes." Common collocations: public consultation, medical consultation, consultation process.
To consider one thing as equal to or the same as another. "Many people mistakenly equate wealth with happiness." Common collocations: equate with, equate to, cannot equate.
The Earth; a spherical representation of Earth. "Technology has connected people across the globe." Common collocations: around the globe, global issues, globe-spanning.

The force that attracts objects toward each other; seriousness or importance. "The gravity of the situation became clear when the results were announced." Common collocations: gravity of the situation, force of gravity, understand the gravity.
As a consequence; for this reason. "The project exceeded the budget; hence, additional funding was required." Common collocations: hence the need, hence why, and hence.
Exactly alike; showing no difference. "The two samples were identical in every measurable aspect." Common collocations: identical twins, virtually identical, identical copies.
To bring about or cause something to happen; to persuade. "The medication is designed to induce sleep in patients with insomnia." Common collocations: induce change, induce labor, induce someone.
To place, fit, or add something into something else. "Please insert your card into the machine to complete the transaction." Common collocations: insert a coin, insert text, insert into.
To cite or appeal to someone or something as an authority; to call upon. "The lawyer invoked precedent to support her argument." Common collocations: invoke a law, invoke the right, invoke authority.
In the same way; also; similarly. "The first experiment succeeded, and likewise the second trial produced positive results." Common collocations: likewise for, do likewise, and likewise.

An agency or means of doing something; a middle position or state. "Television is an effective medium for reaching large audiences." Common collocations: communication medium, medium of exchange, medium-sized.
To make partial changes to something; to alter. "Researchers had to modify their approach based on preliminary results." Common collocations: modify the design, modify behavior, genetically modify.

Experienced or done by each of two or more parties toward the other. "The partnership is based on mutual respect and shared goals." Common collocations: mutual understanding, mutual benefit, mutual agreement.

In spite of; nevertheless. "Notwithstanding the challenges, the team completed the project on time." Common collocations: notwithstanding the fact, provisions notwithstanding, anything notwithstanding.

The central and most important part of something; the core. "The family serves as the nucleus of social organization in many cultures." Common collocations: cell nucleus, nucleus of activity, form a nucleus.
To counterbalance or compensate for something. "The company plants trees to offset its carbon emissions." Common collocations: offset costs, offset by, offset the impact.

To align or position something in relation to surroundings; to familiarize with a situation. "New employees attend a program to orient themselves with company policies." Common collocations: orient toward, orient oneself, orient the discussion.
To extend over and cover part of something; to have elements in common. "There is significant overlap between the two research areas." Common collocations: overlap with, overlap in, areas of overlap.

A limit or boundary that defines the scope of something; a measurable factor. "The study operated within strict ethical parameters." Common collocations: set parameters, within parameters, key parameters.
Accepting what happens without active response or resistance. "Passive smoking can have serious health consequences." Common collocations: passive voice, passive resistance, passive role.

The study of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, and values; a set of guiding principles. "The company's philosophy emphasizes sustainability and social responsibility." Common collocations: business philosophy, philosophy of education, ancient philosophy.

To present or constitute a problem or challenge; to adopt a particular position. "Climate change poses a significant threat to biodiversity." Common collocations: pose a threat, pose a question, pose challenges.
To come before something in time, order, or position. "A brief introduction will precede the main presentation." Common collocations: precede by, immediately precede, precede the event.

Occurring before or in preparation for something more important. "Preliminary results suggest a strong correlation between the variables." Common collocations: preliminary findings, preliminary investigation, preliminary stage.

To suppose something is true without proof; to take for granted. "It would be wrong to presume that all students learn at the same pace." Common collocations: presume that, presume to, reasonably presume.
Widespread in a particular area or at a particular time. "Malaria remains prevalent in tropical regions." Common collocations: increasingly prevalent, most prevalent, prevalent view.

Something regarded as more important than other things; the right to proceed before others. "Environmental protection should be a national priority." Common collocations: top priority, give priority, priority list.
To formally forbid something by law or rule. "Local regulations prohibit smoking in all public buildings." Common collocations: prohibit from, strictly prohibit, prohibit the use.

The act of making information available to the public; a published work. "The publication of the report sparked widespread debate." Common collocations: academic publication, publication date, upon publication.
To buy something; the act of buying. "Consumers can purchase products online with greater convenience." Common collocations: purchase price, purchase decision, make a purchase.
To follow or continue with an activity or course of action. "She decided to pursue a career in medicine." Common collocations: pursue a goal, pursue education, actively pursue.
To settle or find a solution to a problem; firm determination. "The committee resolved the dispute through mediation." Common collocations: resolve a conflict, resolve issues, resolve to do.

A projected sequence of events or a possible situation. "In the worst-case scenario, the project could be delayed by months." Common collocations: worst-case scenario, possible scenario, realistic scenario.
The extent of the area or subject matter that something deals with. "The scope of the research was limited to urban areas." Common collocations: scope of, broad scope, beyond the scope.

A particular order in which related events or things follow each other. "The sequence of events leading to the crisis was carefully documented." Common collocations: in sequence, sequence of events, logical sequence.
